body:
Response begins when danger threatens or occurs

When a disaster is imminent or has occurred, the immediate priority is to protect life and meet urgent needs. The activities undertaken at this stage are called response.

Response consists of actions taken directly before, during or after a disaster to save lives, reduce injury and health impacts, ensure public safety and meet the basic subsistence needs of affected people.

Examples include warning and evacuating threatened residents, conducting rescue operations, arranging urgent medical assistance and restoring essential emergency communications. A response can begin before the physical hazard strikes, as happens when people are evacuated ahead of a cyclone.

Relief meets immediate essential needs

Relief refers to assistance provided to people affected by a disaster, particularly to meet urgent needs. Common relief measures include temporary shelter, food, safe drinking water, essential clothing, sanitation and medical support.

Response and relief are closely connected but are not identical. Response is the broader immediate action to protect people and deal with the emergency. Relief focuses on assistance to affected people. Rescue operations, for example, are response activities; supplying drinking water and essential provisions to evacuated families is relief.

Relief must also be accessible and fair. Children, older people, persons with disabilities and others who have particular needs may require additional assistance. Providing basic necessities without discrimination and ensuring safe, dignified conditions are important elements of humane disaster relief.

Recovery restores or improves community life

Recovery covers the restoration or improvement of the economic, physical, social, cultural and environmental systems and activities of a disaster-affected community. It is wider than simply repairing damaged buildings.

For example, recovery after a flood may involve reopening schools, restoring drinking-water systems, helping households resume livelihoods and repairing essential transport links. Recovery often begins while relief is continuing and may extend over a long period.

Rehabilitation restores basic functioning

Rehabilitation concerns restoring the basic services, facilities and capacities needed for community life. Reopening a health centre, restoring school facilities and enabling essential public services to function again are examples.

Reconstruction rebuilds damaged infrastructure

Reconstruction concerns rebuilding and restoring damaged housing, infrastructure, facilities and services. Reconstructing a destroyed bridge or rebuilding permanent homes illustrates this activity.

The difference is one of emphasis: rehabilitation restores the capacity to function, whereas reconstruction focuses on rebuilding what is needed for sustained functioning. Both can form part of the wider recovery process.

The phases form a continuing cycle

The disaster-management cycle is commonly explained through pre-disaster risk reduction and preparedness, followed by response, relief, recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction. This is a useful way to organise the subject, but the activities do not occur in completely separate periods.

Preparations for future emergencies may be improved during recovery. Mitigation measures can be incorporated into reconstruction. Temporary relief may continue while permanent housing is being built.

Build Back Better

Build Back Better means using recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction to reduce future disaster risk rather than simply restoring the conditions that existed before the disaster.

For instance, rebuilding a damaged settlement in the same vulnerable condition may recreate the earlier risk. Safer building locations, better access routes, improved drainage and stronger essential services can make future losses less likely.

The concept does not mean that rebuilding must wait until every other recovery activity has ended. Risk reduction should be considered while recovery decisions are being made.

Prelims focus

  • Response can take place directly before, during or after a disaster.
  • Relief addresses urgent needs such as shelter, food, water and medical assistance.
  • Rehabilitation restores essential services and capacities.
  • Reconstruction rebuilds damaged infrastructure and facilities.
  • Recovery is broader than reconstruction and includes livelihoods and community functioning.
  • Trap: The disaster-management cycle is not a strictly one-way sequence.

[Sources: Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025, section 2, definitions of response, recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction, and section 5, minimum-relief provisions inserted in section 6 of the principal Act; United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, Sendai Framework Terminology on Disaster Risk Reduction, 2017, entries Disaster Management, Recovery, Rehabilitation and Reconstruction, consulted 2 November 2026; Disaster Management Act, 2005, sections 2, 30 and 41.]

title: After a Disaster: Response, Relief, Rehabilitation, Recovery and Reconstruction

body:
Why a legal framework is necessary

Disasters may simultaneously affect transport, electricity, drinking water, health services, agriculture, housing and communications. Managing these consequences requires different departments and levels of government to act together. A legal framework establishes institutions, identifies responsibilities, provides for plans and funds, and supports coordinated action.

India's principal national legislation is the Disaster Management Act, 2005, Act 53 of 2005, dated 23 December 2005. It provides for disaster management at the national, state, district and local levels.

Its central idea is that disaster management is a continuous and integrated process. It includes prevention, risk reduction, capacity-building, preparedness, response, assessment, evacuation, relief, recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction.

The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025

The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 is Act 10 of 2025. It received presidential assent on 29 March 2025. The Central Government's notification dated 8 April 2025 brought its provisions into force on 9 April 2025.

The amendment revised several definitions and altered the distribution of responsibilities among institutions. The following distinctions reflect the legislation in force at the content cutoff of 2 November 2026.

AreaImportant change in 2025
DefinitionsExpress definitions added or revised for disaster risk, hazard, exposure, vulnerability, resilience, response, recovery and related terms.
Risk reductionDisaster management expressly includes disaster-risk reduction.
National and state plansNational and State Disaster Management Authorities received clearer responsibility for coordinating preparation and approval.
National committeesThe National Crisis Management Committee and High Level Committee received express statutory recognition.
Urban governanceProvision added for Urban Disaster Management Authorities in specified cities.
Response forcesProvision added allowing state governments to constitute State Disaster Response Forces.
Disaster informationNational and state disaster databases expressly incorporated into the legal framework.

Disaster-risk reduction is part of development

The amended Act expressly connects disaster-risk reduction with lowering exposure, reducing vulnerability and improving preparedness, resilience and capacity. This means that disaster management is not solely the responsibility of emergency responders.

For example, the department responsible for roads must consider relevant disaster risks when planning and maintaining roads. A local authority must consider safety standards in construction under its jurisdiction. Health and water-supply agencies must prepare to continue essential functions when services are disrupted.

The law therefore supports mainstreaming disaster-risk reduction: considering hazards and vulnerability during ordinary planning and development, rather than treating disasters only as exceptional events.

Two important legal qualifications

Human-induced disasters are covered, but law-and-order situations are excluded

The law is not confined to earthquakes and cyclones. Industrial accidents and other qualifying human-induced occurrences can also fall within its scope. However, the 2025 amendment explicitly clarifies that human-made causes in the statutory disaster definition do not include law-and-order-related matters or situations arising from them.

Permission to create a body is not the same as creating it

Some institutional provisions are mandatory, while others are enabling provisions. For instance, the 2025 amendment says that a state government may establish an Urban Disaster Management Authority for eligible cities and may constitute a State Disaster Response Force. Their actual establishment depends on the required state notification. The amendment does not automatically establish those bodies in every eligible city or state.

Prelims focus

  • Disaster Management Act, 2005: Act 53 of 2005.
  • Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025: Act 10 of 2025.
  • Presidential assent to the 2025 amendment: 29 March 2025.
  • Commencement of the 2025 amendment: 9 April 2025.
  • The 2025 amendment expressly recognises the National Crisis Management Committee and High Level Committee.
  • Trap: The statutory provision for an Urban Disaster Management Authority does not mean one exists automatically in every qualifying city.

[Sources: Disaster Management Act, 2005, Act 53 of 2005, preamble and sections 1–2; Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025, Act 10 of 2025, sections 1–2, 5–8, 10, 14, 22–23 and 26; Ministry of Home Affairs, Gazette notification S.O. 1648(E), 8 April 2025; Ministry of Home Affairs, Press Information Bureau, Disaster Management (Amendment) Bill, 2024, parliamentary reply dated 22 July 2025. Legislative position checked against these sources on 2 November 2026.]

title: India's Disaster Management Law: The 2005 Act and the 2025 Amendment

body:
The National Disaster Management Authority

The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) is India's apex national body for disaster-management policy and guidance. Under section 3 of the Disaster Management Act, 2005, it is chaired by the Prime Minister. The Act provides for the Chairperson and not more than 9 other members.

NDMA's principal responsibilities include laying down disaster-management policies, plans and guidelines, promoting risk reduction, providing technical guidance and overseeing the broad national approach to preparedness and recovery.

Under the framework amended in 2025, NDMA also coordinates the preparation and approval of the National Disaster Management Plan, in consultation with the Central Government, state governments and other relevant stakeholders.

The National Executive Committee

The National Executive Committee (NEC) assists the national framework with coordination, monitoring and implementation. It is chaired by the Secretary to the Government of India in charge of the ministry or department administering disaster management. At the national level, the Ministry of Home Affairs has the principal coordinating role.

The NEC coordinates preparedness and response measures involving central ministries and agencies, monitors implementation of plans and may coordinate action when a disaster affects more than one state.

NDMA and NEC must not be confused. NDMA is the apex policy and planning authority. NEC performs important executive coordination and monitoring functions. Older descriptions assigning preparation of the National Plan to NEC must be read in light of the 2025 amendment, which revised the relevant planning responsibilities.

The National Crisis Management Committee

The National Crisis Management Committee (NCMC) is chaired by the Cabinet Secretary. Section 8A, inserted by the 2025 amendment, recognises it as the nodal body for dealing with major disasters having serious or national ramifications.

The NCMC is not a replacement for the NDMA or the NEC. Its role concerns high-level crisis management and coordination when the scale and consequences of a major disaster require it.

The High Level Committee

The High Level Committee (HLC), recognised under section 8B, is chaired by the Union Minister in charge of the ministry or department administering disaster management.

Its central distinction is financial assistance. The HLC deals with assistance to state governments envisaged under section 46 and approves financial assistance for mitigation needs under section 47.

Thus, the NCMC is associated with major-crisis management, whereas the HLC is associated with disaster-related financial assistance decisions.

The National Institute of Disaster Management

The National Institute of Disaster Management (NIDM) is the national institution for training, research, documentation, education and capacity-building in disaster management under section 42 of the Act.

NIDM develops training and educational materials, supports research and assists institutions and governments in strengthening disaster-management knowledge and capability. It should not be confused with a rescue force.

The National Disaster Response Force

The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), provided for under section 44, is a specialist force for responding to threatening disaster situations and disasters.

Its operational purpose is distinct from the role of NIDM. NDRF is a response force; NIDM is a training and research institute.

How national institutions work together

National disaster governance is not a simple chain in which each institution performs the same function. Policy, interdepartmental coordination, major-crisis management, financial decisions, specialist response and capacity-building are different responsibilities.

The Central Government and its ministries retain responsibilities for their respective sectors. Forecasting agencies produce hazard information; ministries responsible for essential services support preparedness and continuity; specialist responders support affected areas when required.

In ordinary disaster-response arrangements, the state government has primary responsibility for rescue, relief and rehabilitation in its territory. The Central Government supplements state efforts with financial, logistical and specialist support when required. A serious disaster therefore involves coordination between national and state institutions rather than an automatic transfer of every local responsibility to New Delhi.

Prelims focus

  • NDMA: chaired by the Prime Minister; apex national policy and planning authority.
  • NEC: chaired by the Secretary in charge of the central disaster-management ministry or department; coordination and monitoring.
  • NCMC: chaired by the Cabinet Secretary; major disasters with serious or national ramifications.
  • HLC: chaired by the Union Minister responsible for disaster management; disaster-related financial assistance decisions.
  • NIDM: training, research and capacity-building; NDRF: specialist disaster response.
  • Trap: NDRF and NIDM are not interchangeable institutions.

[Sources: Disaster Management Act, 2005, sections 3, 6, 8, 10, 42 and 44; Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025, sections 5–8, inserting sections 8A and 8B and revising sections 6 and 10; Ministry of Home Affairs, Press Information Bureau, parliamentary reply on the 2025 amendment and central-state coordination, 22 July 2025; National Disaster Management Authority, SACHET National Disaster Alert Portal, About, consulted 2 November 2026.]
